title: Gaussian (Normal) Distribution
statusNote: Reference slice implemented and locally verified. Independent scientific and educational review and Founder acceptance are pending, so this module is not accepted.
summary: A continuous, symmetric, two-parameter distribution on the real line, used as the default model for measurement noise and as a building block for many larger probabilistic models.

sections.title: Plain-language definition
sections.markdown:
The **Gaussian distribution** — also called the **normal distribution** — is a continuous probability distribution on the whole real line. It is fixed by two numbers: a location parameter **μ** (the mean) and a scale parameter **σ > 0** (the standard deviation).

Its probability *density* is a symmetric bell centred at μ: values near μ are more plausible than values far away, and the curve falls off smoothly in both directions. Because X is continuous, the probability of any exact value is zero. We work with density, and probabilities come from areas under the curve.

A random variable X with this distribution is written X ~ N(μ, σ²). The second parameter in that notation is the **variance**, not the standard deviation.

sections.title: Problem and motivation
sections.markdown:
Many quantities are modelled as a central value plus symmetric noise: a measured length, a sensor reading, a residual in a regression, or the average of many small independent effects. The Gaussian gives a compact, mathematically tractable description of that situation.

The **central limit theorem** explains part of its ubiquity: suitably standardised sums or averages of many independent contributions approach a Gaussian distribution under mild conditions. This is a statement about the *scaled average*, not a guarantee that raw data are Gaussian.

That default status is also the main risk. Real data can be skewed, bounded, multi-modal, discrete or heavy-tailed. The Gaussian is a model with assumptions, not a universal description of randomness.

sections.title: Visual intuition
sections.markdown:
Use the laboratory below. **μ** slides the curve left and right without changing its shape. **σ** stretches or compresses the curve horizontally: larger σ means more spread and a lower peak, because the total area under a density curve must remain exactly 1.

The plot shows the density on the fixed window x ∈ [−12, 12]. The Gaussian has no finite support: the curve continues beyond the window toward zero but never reaches it. The window is a display choice, not a claim that values outside it are impossible.

The shaded-looking intuition to keep in mind is **area**, not height. The area between μ − σ and μ + σ is about 68.27% of the total probability; between μ − 2σ and μ + 2σ about 95.45%; between μ − 3σ and μ + 3σ about 99.73%.

sections.title: Structure of the model
sections.markdown:
| Component | Gaussian |
| --- | --- |
| Random variable | X ∈ ℝ (continuous) |
| Parameters | μ ∈ ℝ, σ > 0 |
| Support | The entire real line, (−∞, ∞) |
| Density | Symmetric, unimodal, strictly positive everywhere |
| Mean | E[X] = μ |
| Variance | Var(X) = σ² |
| Shape | Determined by σ; no separate skewness or tail parameter |
| Cumulative distribution | Φ((x − μ) / σ), with no elementary closed form |

The family is closed under linear transformations: if X ~ N(μ, σ²) then aX + b ~ N(aμ + b, a²σ²). Standardising, Z = (X − μ) / σ, gives the standard normal N(0, 1), whose CDF is written Φ.

sections.title: Symbols and equations
sections.markdown:
| Symbol | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| X | The random variable being modelled |
| x | A particular real value at which the density is evaluated |
| μ | Location parameter; also the mean |
| σ | Scale parameter; the standard deviation, in the same units as X |
| σ² | Variance, in squared units |
| f(x) | Probability density; not a probability |
| Φ(z) | Standard normal cumulative distribution function |

Density integrates to probability: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx. For a very small interval of width dx, f(x)·dx approximates the probability of landing in it. Density values may exceed 1 when σ is small; probabilities cannot.

sections.title: Where the formula comes from
sections.markdown:
Start from the standard normal density g(z) = C·exp(−z²/2). Requiring total area 1 gives C = 1/√(2π), because the Gaussian integral ∫ exp(−z²/2) dz over the real line equals √(2π) (evaluated by squaring the integral and using polar coordinates).

Now set z = (x − μ)/σ. A change of variables contributes the Jacobian factor 1/σ, so the density of X is (1/σ)·g((x − μ)/σ). Substituting g gives the formula shown above. The exponent measures squared standardised distance from the mean; the prefactor 1/(σ√(2π)) is exactly what keeps the area equal to 1 as σ changes.

This also shows why the peak height is 1/(σ√(2π)): at x = μ the exponent is zero, so the density reaches its maximum there, and increasing σ lowers that maximum.

sections.title: Fitting, inference and sampling
sections.markdown:
**Maximum likelihood.** For independent observations x₁, …, xₙ, the log-likelihood is maximised by the sample mean for μ and by the average squared deviation for σ²:

- μ̂ = (1/n) Σ xᵢ
- σ̂² = (1/n) Σ (xᵢ − μ̂)²

The variance estimator with denominator **n** is the maximum likelihood estimator. It is biased downward in finite samples; the unbiased sample variance uses denominator **n − 1**. Reporting which denominator is used matters, especially for small n.

**Inference.** A confidence interval for μ uses the standard error σ/√n (with a t correction when σ is estimated from small samples). Bayesian inference combines a prior with the likelihood; a conjugate normal prior yields a normal posterior. Neither procedure is implemented as an interactive laboratory in M001 — the statements here are explanatory.

**Sampling.** Exact samplers exist: inverse-CDF (Box–Muller is a classical transform-based method) and library samplers such as `scipy.stats.norm.rvs`. This milestone does not generate observations in the browser, and the plot contains no simulated data. Sampling behaviour should be studied with a documented seed and a stated sample size.

sections.title: Runnable code
sections.markdown:
The export below reproduces the **current** parameter snapshot and the same display window using NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib. `--json` prints the parameters, mean, variance, peak density and the full sampled curve; `--plot PATH` writes a PNG.

The script is a downloadable, standalone file. Python is **not** executed in the browser, and this repository does not expose an arbitrary code runner. Run it locally in the isolated environment described by `python/requirements.txt`.

sections.title: Applications
sections.markdown:
- Measurement-error and sensor-noise models.
- Residual models inside regression and state-space methods such as the Kalman filter.
- Components of mixture models and latent-variable models.
- Initialisations and approximate posteriors in variational methods.
- Closed-form baselines before trying heavier-tailed or more flexible models.

In each case the Gaussian is a modelling choice with assumptions. It is often a convenient approximation rather than a literal description of the data-generating process.

sections.title: Assumptions and limitations
sections.markdown:
- **Unbounded support.** Any real value has positive density, including impossible negative values for a strictly positive quantity.
- **Symmetry and a single mode.** Skewed or multi-modal data are poorly represented.
- **Light tails.** Extreme values are far less likely than under a Student's t or other heavy-tailed model.
- **Fixed shape.** There is no separate parameter for skewness or tail weight.
- **Density is not probability.** A density value can exceed 1; only areas are probabilities.
- **The plotted window is finite.** Truncating the display at ±12 does not truncate the distribution, and the visible area is not evidence of exact normalization.
- **Fitted parameters are estimates.** They carry uncertainty that this display does not quantify.
- **No interactive fitting or sampling.** Those topics are explained in text only in M001 and would require their own verified laboratories.

sections.title: Knowledge check
sections.markdown:
1. If σ doubles while μ stays fixed, what happens to the peak height and to the area under the whole curve?
2. Why can a probability density exceed 1, while a probability cannot?
3. A fitted model reports σ̂² using denominator n. Is that the unbiased sample variance?

<details><summary>Answers</summary>

1. The peak height halves because it is 1/(σ√(2π)); the total area stays 1.
2. Density is probability per unit of x. Only its integral over an interval is a probability, and that integral is bounded by 1.
3. No. The maximum likelihood estimator uses denominator n and is biased downward; the unbiased estimator uses n − 1.

</details>
